Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Learning to Infer: Statistical Inference through Meta Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study meta learning for statistical inference, in which neural networks learn inference rules from simulated tasks and apply them to new datasets without parameter updates, providing a form of in-context learning. We draw on statistical decision theory to design training objectives whose population minimizers are Bayes rules and exploit their connections to classical inference procedures to establish frequentist guarantees for the learned rules. The structure of classical inference procedures also motivates the design of our neural network architecture, called Residual Recurrent Deep Sets (RRDS), which repeatedly aggregates information across observations in a permutation-invariant manner and refines its internal state through residual updates. Under suitable regularity and training conditions, we establish asymptotic efficiency in parameter estimation, consistency in model selection, and variable selection guarantees in high-dimensional regression models. The RRDS architecture allows us to avoid the curse of sample size that arises in generic neural network approximation when the network takes the entire dataset as input. For fixed-dimensional models, the network size and the number of meta training tasks need only grow polynomially in the sample size; under additional analyticity conditions, these requirements improve to polylogarithmic growth in network size and nearly linear growth in the number of training tasks. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample advantages of the learned inference rules over classical methods.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Debiased Inference via Posterior Corrections for High-Dimensional Regression
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: There has been significant progress in Bayesian inference based on sparsity-inducing priors, such as spike-and-slab and horseshoe priors, for high-dimensional regression. The resulting posteriors, however, in general do not possess desirable frequentist properties, and the credible sets thus cannot serve as valid confidence sets even asymptotically. We introduce a novel debiasing approach that corrects the bias for the entire (possibly approximate) Bayesian posterior distribution. We establish new Bernstein-von Mises theorems that guarantee the frequentist validity of the debiased law. We demonstrate the practical performance of our proposal through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications in economics.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: When benchmark problems share sources, such as variants of one template or tasks from one repository, an evaluation budget must fix the number of sources as well as the number of problems. We ask whether pilot data or earlier evaluation results can predict, before an evaluation is run, how much the standard deviation (SD) of the score grows when the same budget is concentrated on fewer sources. We use the classical design effect with an intraclass correlation estimated on data disjoint from those used to check the prediction. On GSM-Symbolic, 100 problems drawn as 10 templates x 10 variants have an SD of 9.2 pp against 2.7 pp from 100 templates; pilot data on 15 other questions predict the ratio as 3.49 against 3.52 measured on held-out questions (medians over 20 splits; single splits err by -13% to +16%), once the actual sampling plan is included. On SWE-bench Verified, 10 randomly selected public submissions predict the median ratio for 119 other submissions within 3% for 2 or more repositories, and 3 submissions are nearly as good. Dropping the finite-population terms from the design prediction gives errors of 13-21% on GSM-Symbolic, where it reduces to the textbook formula, and 25-35% on SWE-bench. Widening iid intervals by the square root of the pilot design effect brings pass@1 coverage on concentrated designs to 0.93-0.98, but not pass@16 (0.85, 0.76). We also report two lessons for anyone validating such predictions: split pilot and held-out data by question source, not by difficulty version, and do not read a good fit of the formula as evidence of source clustering (MATH-500). The method is not new; we contribute a held-out test of its advance predictions and a recipe for using them. Code: https://github.com/Guang627/deff-eval

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $ε$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-γ)^{-1},(1-γ)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $γ$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-γ)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $δ\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $τ$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $τ^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $τ=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Sampling with graph wavelet kernels: optimality and adaptivity to regularity and geometry
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-Hölder and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-Hölder observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This survey provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from AI feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: The paper has been accepted by Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Externally Valid Policy Choice
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We consider the problem of estimating personalized treatment policies that are "externally valid" or "generalizable": they perform well in target populations that differ from the experimental (or training) population from which the data are sampled. We first show that welfare-maximizing policies for the experimental population are robust to a certain class of shifts in the distribution of potential outcomes between the experimental and target populations (holding characteristics fixed). We then develop methods for estimating policies that are robust to shifts in the joint distribution of outcomes and characteristics. In doing so, we highlight how treatment effect heterogeneity within the experimental population shapes external validity.

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.comment: 15 pages, preprint

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: Distortion-Corrected Diffusion MRI Using Rotated-View EPI and Joint Field-Map/Image Estimation with Gaussian Primitives
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Echo planar imaging (EPI) is the standard acquisition technique for diffusion and functional neuroimaging, enabling rapid imaging but suffering from geometric distortions caused by B0 field inhomogeneities. Existing correction methods first reconstruct distorted images using parallel imaging, then estimate the B0 field and correct the distortion in the image domain. In this sequential process, reconstruction artifacts at high acceleration factors and low SNR at high diffusion b-values degrade B0 estimation and limit the overall correction quality. We propose a physics-informed framework that jointly estimates the B0 field, the distortion-free image, and the shot-to-shot phase directly from k-space data, without depending on an intermediate parallel-imaging reconstruction. All three are represented as superpositions of Gaussian primitives embedded within an EPI forward model; the explicit, continuous parameterization captures both smooth regions and tissue boundaries and is evaluated on rotated sampling grids without resampling. The diffusion-weighted image is modeled as real and non-negative, with the image phase absorbed into a per-shot phase factor. Acquiring the blip-up/blip-down data at several phase-encoding orientations, the rotated-view principle of PROPELLER applied to full-FOV single-shot EPI, distributes distortions across orientations, improving point spread function isotropy and providing stronger constraints for B0 estimation. On in vivo brain diffusion EPI at R=4 and 5, the proposed method attains the closest brain-boundary agreement with a distortion-free structural reference, with the largest improvement over sequential methods at high b-value.

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: PRISM: Perceptual Rate-Controllable Extreme Image Compression with Visual State-Space Models
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Generative codecs built on pretrained diffusion priors achieve high perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates (below 0.05 bpp). However, most methods still require a separate model for each bitrate, and offer no control over the amount of detail synthesized. Their rate efficiency also depends on the entropy model, where Mamba-based state-space models (SSMs) have recently improved autoregressive context modeling. However, conventional SSM scans are not aligned with the decoding order, and each decoding pass restarts from an empty state, discarding context accumulated in previous passes. We propose PRISM, an extreme image compression method that addresses these limitations. A single model provides two continuous controls: a rate knob that traverses the rate-distortion curve and a realism knob that adjusts the level of detail synthesized. Its visual state-space (VSS) context model introduces a decode-order-aligned (DOA) scan, which predicts each latent from a state that summarizes all decoded context, and cross-tap state carry, which initializes each tap with a summary of the previous one. Experiments show that PRISM outperforms both variable-rate and fixed-rate codecs, requiring on average 22% less bitrate than the strongest baseline at equal FID while also achieving higher PSNR.

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: SpiderSkel: Sub-Pixel Multi-Tangent 2D Skeletonization from Inscribed-Disc Geometry
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Skeletonization reduces a binary shape to a compact medial representation, but pixel-grid discretization perturbs the boundary-contact geometry underlying the medial axis, creating tension among connectivity, reconstruction fidelity, and skeleton compactness. SpiderSkel is a family of training-free two-dimensional skeletonization methods built on multi-tangent inscribed-disc geometry. A tie-aware exact Euclidean distance transform retains tied nearest boundary sites rather than collapsing them to a single label; medial candidates are localised to sub-pixel positions from the inscribed disc's tangent contacts, filtered by the angular span of those contacts, and completed by connectivity-aware refinement. Across nineteen public benchmarks comprising 11,323 images of shapes, retinal vessels, cracks and roads, and document images, a single operating point fixed across datasets yields skeletons that, on every image, have exact skeleton topology under the component/hole certificate, remain fully connected, and have exact per-object reconstruction topology. The three SpiderSkel variants are the only evaluated methods to satisfy all three properties across every category; within each category, every variant is Pareto-optimal with respect to all twenty-two baselines in strict sub-pixel reconstruction Dice versus reduction rate. Incremental engines for all three variants reproduce the skeleton of a complete recomputation exactly across 23,040 verified edit steps, with median update latencies of 15.4-18.1 ms per foreground edit and 4.3-4.4 ms per canvas edit, and speedups reaching 33.0-fold on canvas edits.
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, plus 6 pages of supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Image Processing

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: Evaluating Cine and Tagged MRI-to-Speech Synthesis with Complementary Metrics and MRI-Free Controls
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Relating tongue motion measured with dynamic MRI to the speech it produces could inform rehabilitation after glossectomy. Prior studies have translated cine or tagged MRI into log-mel spectrograms and used the two-dimensional Pearson correlation between predicted and recorded spectrograms (Corr2D) to quantify the acoustic information captured by each imaging modality. However, Corr2D has not been calibrated against MRI-free predictors that preserve basic acoustic structure. Our contribution is an evaluation framework for speech synthesis from cine MRI, tagged MRI and their combination; the synthesis network is held fixed. On identical leave-one-subject-out folds, we compare four trained input configurations with two MRI-free controls: a static mean-spectrum baseline and a time-aligned cohort template. Across 44 subjects (18 after glossectomy) producing two utterances, the cohort template, which never sees an MRI, reached a Corr2D of 0.745 and 0.664. The static baseline, which contains no timing, reached 87 to 89% of that score. No trained configuration outperformed the template on Corr2D, a cepstral distance or ESTOI; seven of the eight fell significantly short on Corr2D. For cine MRI this held across three positional encodings, an encoder temporal-attention module and a training objective matched to the metric. Cine and tagged MRI differed consistently within subjects, although the direction depended on the metric. Absolute Corr2D alone therefore does not show that a model recovers acoustics from the MRI. The two controls are a reusable method: any study can compute them from its own training recordings, so a model's margin over them measures what its images contribute.
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.comment: Accepted for an invited oral presentation in the Deep Dive session of SPIE Medical Imaging 2027, Vancouver, February 2027. 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: PIRA: Pan-CDN Intra-video Resource Adaptation for Short Video Streaming
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: In large scale short video platforms, CDN resource selection plays a critical role in maintaining Quality of Experience (QoE) while controlling escalating traffic costs. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct in the wild network measurements during video playback in a production short video system. The results reveal that CDNs delivering higher average QoE often come at greater financial cost, yet their connection quality fluctuates even within a single video underscoring a fundamental and dynamic trade off between QoE and cost. However, the problem of sustaining high QoE under cost constraints remains insufficiently investigated in the context of CDN selection for short video streaming. To address this, we propose PIRA, a dynamic resource selection algorithm that optimizes QoE and cost in real time during video playback. PIRA formally integrating QoE and cost by a mathematical model, and introduce a intra video control theoretic CDN resource selection approach which can balance QoE and cost under network dynamics. To reduce the computation overheads, PIRA employs state space pruning and adaptive parameter adjustment to efficiently solve the high dimensional optimization problem. In large scale production experiments involving 450,000 users over two weeks, PIRA outperforms the production baseline, achieving a 2.1% reduction in start up delay, 15.2% shorter rebuffering time, and 10% lower average unit traffic cost, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing user experience and financial cost at scale.

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: MedImgAnnotator: batch wise medical image annotation and preprocessing tool
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: The curation of large cohort datasets for developing deep learning models demands annotating or editing over the AI-predicted labels. However, openly available annotation tools are time-consuming, as they involve complex navigational steps and do not support batch processing. This study aimed to develop a simple, fast, semiautomated batch-annotation tool named MedImgAnnotator. The tool was created by integrating editing tools, image mask pair matching logic, preprocessing functions, object detection tool, and a plugin management system. Its performance was evaluated in terms of active annotation time and ease of use by the developer and 12 users using open-source MR and CT scans. Additionally, the tool had been used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation best performance winner to annotate liver masks from 6412 MRI volumes. The evaluation results showed that MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 (average active annotation time of openly available tools) seconds to 59 seconds. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test of 12 users evaluation results recorded P values of 0.032 and 0.008 for the active annotation time and higher ease of use rating metrics, respectively, indicating that the current tool significantly reduces annotation time and enhances ease of use. Moreover, the tool utilization for annotating different regions of interest from different modality scans and body regions shows its usability across modalities and areas of interest. MedImgAnnotator, which significantly reduces active annotation time for large imaging cohorts, is available as an executable file and as a Python script. Access link: https://ewunateassaye.github.io/developed-tools/medimgannotator.html

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.comment: 17 Pages 7 figures

Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
Image Processing / OCR Preprocessing.summary: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary:
Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation?
  We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits.
  We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964.
  These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Large-scale factor analysis shows machine intelligence is only partially interpretable
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: A common assumption in language model development is that cognitive abilities are organized around a general, domain-free intelligence factor, like fluid intelligence in humans. This assumption is rarely tested directly, and prior attempts have done so only at a much smaller scale. We take a latent variable approach to intelligence in language models, similar to how psychometricians study psychological constructs. Using factor analysis, we analyzed 13,230 published evaluation scores covering 1,618 language models across 456 text-only benchmarks. Because the data are sparse, we triangulate our analysis across different data densifiers and imputation methods. Across the imputations that pass our quality filter, the general factor's share of variance in the summed score ($ω_h$) ranges from 0.04 to 0.76, and its share of the common variance (ECV) from 0.11 to 0.52. A robust pattern across different modes of bias is that 1. same-subject benchmarks are not guaranteed to place closely in vector space, with weak median label cohesion, 2. benchmarks loading highest on $G$ tend to be miscellaneous rather than thematically coherent, and 3. standard "intelligence" benchmarks do not dominate the share of ability variance the general factor explains, and there is a lack of evidence that $G$ is well-proxied by them. We hypothesize that targeting a single conceptual ability has little support, since the first-order abilities it would have to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice. This would mean that, from public benchmark scores alone, general intelligence is hard to define, identify, and target as a single construct in language model development. Future experiments should run training regimes that target both theoretically abstract general ability and tasks with semantic similarity and examine how abilities transfer across test sets of diverse formats.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Large Language Model Agents for Evidence Based Genetic Disease Severity Classification
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Disease severity classification for genetic conditions is subjective and labor-intensive, creating bottlenecks in genomic screening, where commercial panels vary widely in size and overlap. We developed an autonomous AI agent integrating Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to classify 10,211 Human Phenotype Ontology terms. It uses American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG)-endorsed severity guidelines and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) quality-of-life criteria to retrieve PubMed literature, generate interpretable reasoning chains, and independently verify claims. At the phenotype level, using expert-curated cohorts, the agent achieved 93.55% accuracy (MCC 0.9237) with 82.6% to 91.4% of claims supported by direct evidence or valid inferences. Gene-level severity was aggregated across 8,738 pairs, identifying 3,283 autosomal recessive pairs with severe or profound presentations. External validation showed 95.2% concordance with Mackenzie's Mission gene list. This system enables standardized panel design by providing reliable, automated classification supported by direct evidence.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Recurrent-depth language models, such as looped Transformers, repeatedly apply shared network blocks to refine latent representations, enabling additional test-time computation without generating explicit intermediate reasoning tokens. However, recurrent inference repeatedly accesses long contexts: full attention incurs quadratic computation during prefill, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads large key-value (KV) caches, introducing substantial memory traffic and capacity pressure. We study how attention routing evolves across recurrent depth and uncover a consistent separation in convergence timescales: routing-related quantities, including the attention support and the attention distribution, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs. This suggests a two-stage structure in which the model discovers a sparse working set and then refines representations over largely the same routing support. Motivated by this structure, we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps to discover a block-structured working set, and then reuses it as the routing support in later steps while keeping recurrent refinement and within-support attention computation dynamic. By combining sparse recurrent attention with compact KV-cache management, WISE reduces both redundant attention computation and memory movement during inference. Across reasoning and long-context benchmarks, WISE closely approaches full-attention accuracy on key evaluated workloads while outperforming early-static support baselines. At 64K context, our implementation achieves up to a 6.46x decode throughput improvement under GPU memory pressure. Our code is available at https://github.com/tbn5pj/WISE_code.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: BLADE: Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based educational assistants often provide direct answers offering little incentive for students to explore or engage with course materials. We present BLADE (Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based conversational assistant grounded in course-specific content that guides students toward relevant materials through citation-grounded dialogue rather than delivering unsourced solutions. We evaluate BLADE in an advanced undergraduate NLP course with extensive instructional resources, in which locating and synthesizing relevant material is a central challenge. During quizzes, students are assigned to one of three conditions: BLADE only, direct course materials only, or both; we measure performance and resource usage. Results show that students consistently select BLADE over direct materials when both are available, and that quiz performance is highest when students use BLADE alone. In contrast, simultaneous use of both resources is associated with significantly lower performance. No statistically significant difference in quiz performance occurred between assigned resource conditions. These findings show the potential of RAG-based assistants as a citation-grounded interface for applying course content under open-book exam-like conditions, while suggesting that adding direct-material access does not necessarily improve in-task performance.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: To appear, European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL), Athens, Greece, March, 2027

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: Ishita Chakraborty and Xingjian You contributed equally

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: NOLLI: A Difficulty-Calibrated English-Korean Puzzle Benchmark
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: We introduce NOLLI, a procedurally generated, difficulty-calibrated English-Korean puzzle benchmark with 15 puzzle types (25 tasks; 7,500 items). Each instance is seed-regenerable, has a verified unique solution, and is scored deterministically. We calibrate difficulty behaviorally by tuning generator parameters to target accuracy bands on a reference model. NOLLI has three task families: matched direct translations, script adaptations over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and Korean-only cultural or orthographic tasks. We evaluate 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models; gap analyses use the 12 above a 3% overall-accuracy floor. On matched direct translations, English and Korean accuracy is equivalent within a prespecified $\pm 10$ percentage-point margin. Script adaptations behave differently: Korean Cipher trails English by up to 68.7 percentage points, while Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic Korean penalty, and Jamo Composition strongly correlates with Korean Cipher performance. Korean-only tasks are also heterogeneous: rule-application performance varies across models, while Kinship remains below each non-floor model's Korean direct-task baseline. Finally, structural size does not increase from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, showing that size alone is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Do Language Models Need a Trainable Input Embedding Table? Fixed Minimal Token Codes at 1.7B-Class Scale
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: A token must be identifiable before a language model can learn how to use it. Must its input coordinates also be learned? We replace the trainable input table of a decoder-only Transformer with a predetermined 16-bit identifier for each of 49,152 tokens. Repetition lifts the code to width 2048 without a learned projection. We train five models from scratch to 100B prediction targets each: a learned-input control and four fixed-input variants using canonical codes, an invertible recoding, an extra Transformer block, or row-normalized codes. At the endpoint, the four fixed-input models attain 51.44-53.34% HellaSwag normalized accuracy, 70.46-71.49% PIQA accuracy, and 42.29-44.52% LAMBADA accuracy. The normalized model attains the upper endpoint on all three; the learned control scores 57.79%, 72.69%, and 47.72%, respectively. At unchanged depth and parameter count, the normalized model's LAMBADA advantage over canonical codes is 1.80 percentage points at 48.44B targets and 1.77 points at 100B. A complementary smaller-scale study observes successful fixed-code learning across three training seeds per interface. At matched backbone depth, the compact input buffer stores 128 times fewer scalar values than the untied learned input table. The construction separates symbol identification from learned lexical coordinates and provides a working model family in which to study how shared computation builds representations from immutable inputs.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: Accepted to EACL 2027. 22 pages, 8 figures. Project page: https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Deep Delta Learning
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: We introduce Deep Delta Learning (DDL), which replaces the additive residual update of the Transformer with the delta rule applied across depth. A standard sublayer adds its output to the residual stream regardless of what the stream already holds. In DDL, each attention or MLP sublayer selects a direction, reads the state along it, and writes a gated rank-1 correction proportional to the error between a learned target and that readout. A single gate interpolates between skipping the sublayer and overwriting the selected component, and every orthogonal direction stays on the identity path. The same rule extends to a residual stream with several value channels per feature, which enlarges the persistent state of the model while attention and MLP widths stay fixed. In decoder-only language models at GPT-2 small and medium scales, each pretrained on 49.15B FineWeb-Edu tokens, every DDL variant reaches lower validation loss and higher mean one-shot accuracy on eight downstream tasks than the additive baseline, with fewer than 0.3% additional parameters.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Preprint correcting minor typographical errors and clarifying baseline evaluation conditions from the SPIE Defense + Security 2026 proceedings

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $δ$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $δ= 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables; supplementary material included

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: Accepted for publication in Neurocomputing journal

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: SparDA: Sparse Decoupled Attention for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: Sparse attention reduces compute and memory bandwidth for long-context LLM inference. However, two key challenges remain: (1) KV cache capacity still grows with sequence length, and offloading to CPU memory introduces a PCIe transfer bottleneck; (2) sparse selection during prefill retains $O(T^2)$ complexity and can dominate attention cost at long contexts. We propose SparDA, a decoupled sparse attention architecture that introduces a fourth per-layer projection, the Forecast, alongside Query, Key, and Value. The Forecast predicts the KV blocks needed by the next layer, enabling lookahead selection that overlaps CPU-to-GPU prefetch with current-layer execution. Because Forecast is decoupled from the attention query, our GQA implementation uses one Forecast head per GQA group, reducing selection overhead versus the original multi-head selector. On the evaluated 8B models, SparDA adds <0.5% parameters and trains only the Forecast projections using attention-derived supervision from the frozen backbone. On two sparse-pretrained 8B models, SparDA maintains accuracy comparable to the full-query sparse-attention baseline while delivering up to 1.25$\times$ prefill speedup and 1.7$\times$ decode speedup over the sparse-attention offload baseline. By enabling larger feasible batch sizes on a single GPU, SparDA further reaches up to 5.3$\times$ higher decode throughput than the non-offload sparse baseline on MiniCPM4.1-8B. Our adaptation to GLM-5.1 (754B MoE) also achieves accuracy comparable to native token-level DSA, extending the accuracy evaluation beyond block-sparse 8B models. Our source code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/SparDA.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.comment: 35 pages, 18 figures, 23 tables, including supplementary material

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Task-Dependent Linguistic Measures in Aphasia Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of Narrative, Descriptive, and Procedural Speech
Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.summary:
Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific elicitation task, and studies use different tasks, so values from different tasks may not be comparable.
  Aims: To test whether discourse tasks change these measures within the same speakers, and whether the measures follow a gradient from Procedural to Descriptive to Narrative discourse. Methods & Procedures: Baseline transcripts from 61 adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia were taken from the Fridriksson-2 corpus in AphasiaBank (POLAR trial, registered as NCT03416738). Each speaker produced a Procedural (Sandwich), a Descriptive (Broken Window) and a Narrative (Cinderella) sample in one session. A rule-based pipeline extracted 13 measures, 10 of which were common enough to test. Friedman, Page and Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction were used, with a speaker-grouped Random Forest classifier as a supporting check.
  Outcomes & Results: Total words and number of different words followed the full gradient, but the step from Procedural to Descriptive was small. For most other measures, Narrative stood apart, while Descriptive and Procedural did not differ. Among the 31 speakers with at least 25 words in every task, filler rate, repetition rate and total disfluency density were higher in Narrative than in both other tasks. The classifier reached an accuracy of 0.61 (always guessing the most common task would give 0.41), mainly by recognizing Narrative samples.
  Conclusions: Discourse tasks are not interchangeable, and expressing disfluencies per word does not remove the task effect. The task should be reported with every measure, and values should be compared only within the same task.

Document Understanding / NLP / Long Text.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
